docs.title: Doxa
docs.text:
Everything is real and is not real,
Both real and not real,
Neither real nor not real.
This is Lord Buddha’s teaching.

- Nāgārjuna
    Verses on the Middle Way (2nd–3rd century CE)

Doxa is a simple to write, highly readible language based on four corned logical values inspired by the logic of Nagarjuna. In Doxa there are no booleans. Doxa instead uses a four cournered logical unit called a tetra. Tetras can represent true and false, which act as you would expect them to in a traditional programing language.

docs.title: Alias
docs.text:
Alias Parameters (^)

Overview Alias parameters allow a function to modify a caller’s variable directly, without general-purpose pointers or references. They are opt-in at both the function signature and call site, making mutations explicit and safe. Aliases are stack-bound, cannot escape their defining function, and cannot be taken from partial subfields or array elements.

Syntax 

fn modify(^param :: int) {
param += 1 # Directly mutates caller's variable
}

var x = 0
modify(^x) # Caller opts-in to mutation
# x == 1
Core Rules

Parameter-only — ^T may only appear in function parameters, never in locals, returns, or stored types. The one other place `^` is written is the collection of an `each` loop (below).

Lvalue-only — Only full variables can be aliased no temporaries, expressions, struct fields, or array elements.

Explicit call-site — Caller must pass ^var to grant mutation rights.

No alias duplication — The same variable cannot be passed to more than one alias parameter in the same call.

No alias + by-value mix — A variable cannot be passed aliased and by-value in the same call.

No escaping — Aliases cannot be returned, stored, or captured by closures.

No async/threads — Aliases are banned in async functions and cannot be passed to concurrent tasks.

Exclusive borrow — Aliases grant exclusive mutable access for the duration of the call no overlapping borrows allowed.

Evaluation order — Arguments evaluate left-to-right, but banned alias patterns remain errors.

Example: Safe Swap

fn swap(^a :: int, ^b :: int) { let tmp is a a is b b is tmp }

var x is 1, y is 2 swap(^x, ^y)

docs.title: x == 2, y == 1
docs.text:
Example: Compile-time Error Cases

swap(^x, ^x) # ❌ same variable passed twice modify(^(x + 1)) # ❌ temporaries not allowed f(^obj.field) # ❌ partial object aliasing not allowed g(^x, x) # ❌ aliased and by-value in same call

Types An alias argument lends its storage, so the callee may both read it and store into it. Its type must therefore be exactly the parameter's (E1025): a narrower variable could be handed a value it cannot hold, and a wider one could be read as something it is not.

function reset(^x :: int | string) {
    x is 0
}

var s :: string is "hi"
reset(^s) # ❌ reset may store an int into a string

The one exception is a union parameter that preserves its member: every store into it goes through a narrowing of it to a single member (as, or a match arm), so it only ever stores back the member it was found to hold. A narrowing to a smaller union, such as the else of x as int on an int | string | float, does not count. Such a parameter may be lent a variable of any one member type, and the variable keeps its type.

function exclaim(^x :: int | string) {
    match x {
        string then x is x + "!",
        int then x is x + 1,
    }
}

var s :: string is "hi"
exclaim(^s) # ✓ s is "hi!"

This is what lets std.methods.push, insert and clear take any collection.

Lending a union parameter on to another counts as storing through it: it preserves its member only if the parameter it is lent to does. A call through a function value cannot be checked against the callee's body, so it never takes a member-typed variable for a union parameter.

Loops: each n in ^path A plain each n in items binds a copy of each element, as every plain store does. Written on the collection, ^ lends it to the loop body, which then changes the elements through n:

each p in ^game.players {
    p.score is p.score + 1   # writes game.players[i]
}
  • The collection is a path: a variable, or this, followed by struct fields (^items, ^game.players, ^this.items). A call, an index, or a view is not one (E3005); bind it to a variable first.
  • While the loop runs, the body may not write, resize, lend, or borrow again the path, anything that holds it, or anything under it (E3006). Changes go through n, which may itself be written, lent (f(^n)), or borrowed by an inner loop (each c in ^n.cells).
  • n is the element, read afresh on every use: a change to the collection the check cannot see, such as a callee that empties a borrowed global, meets a bounds check, never a stale element.
  • Storing or returning n copies it.

Design Intent This model offers mutation semantics without full pointers, preserving deterministic lifetime and memory safety under stack-based allocation. By forcing explicit syntax and disallowing escaping or partial aliasing, it avoids common pitfalls of traditional references while retaining enough flexibility for in-place updates.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays are dynamic by default. They are declared by adding square brackets after the type. Nested arrays are declared by using multiple brackets. By default arrays are stored on the heap.

var arr :: int [] is [1, 2, 3, 4]
var n_arr :: int[][] is [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

@print("{arr[1]}") # 2
@print("{n_arr[0][1]}") # 2

Arrays can be given fixed sizes within type declarations. When given a fixed size, arrays are stored on the stack.

var chessboard :: string[8][8] # 8x8 string matrix on stack
var buffer :: int[256] # 256 integers on stack

If an array is made constant it is stored statically and refrenced by pointer.

const medals is ["gold", "silver", "bronze"]

Arrays are handled by intrinsic methods such as @push, @pop, @slice, etc. An index out of bounds, read or written, and a @pop of an empty array are runtime faults (Runtime faults); the standard library's methods sublibrary has versions that check first.

Arrays will be automatically cast into the requested array storage if possible.

var dyn_arr is [1, 2, 3] # heap allocated
var fixed_arr :: int[3] is dyn_arr # copy is made to the stack
const static_arr is fixed_arr # static allocation made and refrenced

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Dynamic arrays are allocated from the current scope's arena. Array elements are stored in a single contiguous allocation, and mutations that require dynamic storage conversion copy the element data in bulk. Assigning one array variable to another copies it: the two never share elements (see memory.md). A fresh array (a literal, a call's result) is moved, not copied. To change an array somewhere else, lend it with ^: a ^ parameter, or each n in ^arr to change its elements in a loop.

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text: Doxa unifies conditional branching with a consistent then / else pattern across if, as, and match.

docs.title: Branch bodies
docs.text:
Every then and else branch, and every match arm, takes a body in one of three forms:

  • An expression, ending with a space.
  • A block, { ... }, ending without one.
  • A bare return, break, or continue.

The third form is shorthand for the block that contains only that statement, so it diverges exactly as else { continue } does:

const v is maybeInt(s) as int else continue   # same as: else { continue }
if list[i] != "" then n += 1 else continue
match tag {
    "a" then out is 1,
    else continue
}

A bare control statement is newline-terminated, except that else and , may follow it — else belongs to the enclosing branch and , to the next match arm.

docs.title: if / then / else
docs.text:
• then required, else optional for a statement if.
  • An if whose value is used (a declaration's initializer, an argument, an operand) needs an else: without one the false path has no value, and the compiler rejects it (E1038).

Examples:

if x > 10 then {
    @print("x is greater than 10\n")
} else {
    @print("x is 10 or less\n")
}

var condition is if true then "true" else "false"

Chaining and statement-style:

if current % 3 equals 0 and current % 5 equals 0 then @print("fizzbuzz\n")
else if current % 3 equals 0 then @print("fizz\n")
else if current % 5 equals 0 then @print("buzz\n")
else @print("{current}\n")

docs.title: as / then / else (type narrowing)
docs.text:
• else required, then optional.
  • Same body rules: expression bodies end with , block bodies do not.
  • The tested variable is narrowed in both branches: the then branch narrows to the target type, the else branch narrows to the remainder (union minus target).
  • A struct field narrows the same way, in place: inside h.val as int then { … }, reads of h.val are int. The struct itself keeps its type, so h is still a Holder there, and a copy of it (var k is h) is an ordinary Holder.

Examples:

# Inline fallback value
const n_or_zero is value as int else 0

# The fallback is typed by the `as`: `[]` is an empty `string[]`
const names is maybeNames() as string[] else []

# Block with explicit return (guard pattern)
const n is value as int else {
    @print("value is not an int\n")
    return -1
}

# Block with lift (provides fallback value, continues)
const n is value as int else {
    @print("value is not an int, using default\n")
    lift 0
}

# Type narrowing in both branches
const val :: int | float | Error is foo()
val as int then {
    # val :: int here
} else {
    # val :: float | Error here
}

Then block behavior: when the then branch is a block, it runs for side effects only. The as expression's value on the success path is the original narrowed value. When the then branch is an inline expression, its value is used as the result.

var x is val as int then 20 else 0        # x is 20 (inline then)
var x is val as int then { work() } else 0 # x is val's int value (block then, side-effects)

docs.title: Block values and lift
docs.text:
In if and as branches, blocks do not implicitly return their last expression. The last expression in a block is discarded (side-effect only). To provide a value from a block, use lift:

# lift provides a value from a block
var x is if cond then { lift compute() } else { lift 0 }

# Without lift, blocks produce nothing — use inline for simple values
var x is if cond then compute() else 0

lift terminates the block (code after lift is unreachable). It scopes to the immediately enclosing block { }.

return always exits the enclosing function. lift always provides a value to the enclosing expression. break and continue always target the innermost enclosing loop.

var x is foo() as int else {
    @print("error\n")
    lift 0               # x gets 0, execution continues after the as expression
}

var x is foo() as int else {
    @print("fatal\n")
    return -1            # function exits, x is never assigned
}

When as or if is used in assignment, block branches must either lift a value or diverge via return/break/continue. A block that falls through without lift produces nothing, which is a compile error when a value is expected. A branch that is a bare control statement counts as diverging here too, since it is the same block written without braces.

match arms are not affected — implicit last-expression returns are preserved in match blocks.

docs.title: if vs as
docs.text:
In Doxa, if and as both use the then / else pattern, but they invert the emphasis:

Keyword Requires Optional Implied meaning if then else If success then do x, failure branch optional as else then As a type or else do x, success branch optional

if is a keyword which implicitly requires a success condition, as implicity requires a fail condition, but both use then/else blocks in the same way.

Examples

# IF: Truth-driven
if x > 10 then @print("big\n") else @print("small\n")

# AS: Fallback-driven
value as int else 0         # If not int, use 0
value as int then 20 else 0  # If int, use 20  else 0

# Both in action
if isReady then start() else wait()
data as string then parse(data) else log("Bad data\n")

docs.title: match (values and union types)
docs.text:
Use match to branch on:

  • Concrete values: numbers, strings, enum variants (.Red, .Green, ...)
  • Union type arms: int, float, string, byte, tetra, nothing, or custom types
  • Struct subjects: the struct's name as a type test, optionally with a { field } pattern to bind its fields

Arm syntax and delimiters:

  • Pattern arms: pattern then BODY
  • Else arm: else BODY (no then)
  • Body: expression (end with ) or block { ... } (no trailing )

Match on union types:

fn kind(value :: int | float) returns(string) {
    return match value {
        int then @print("integer\n")
        float then @print("float\n")
    }
}

Match on enums and values:

enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }

var msg1 is match color {
    .Red then "It's red"
    .Blue then "It's blue"
    else "It's something else"
}

const x is 5
var msg2 is match x {
    0 then "It's zero"
    5 then "It's five"
    else "It's something else"
}

const s is "big"
var msg3 is match s {
    "big" then "It's big"
    "small" then "It's small"
    else "It's something else"
}

Match on structs:

struct FileError { public path :: string }

var e :: FileError is $FileError { path is "a.txt" }

match e {
    FileError then @print("it failed\n"),          # type test: the subject is that struct
}

match e {
    FileError { path } then @print(path + "\n"),   # binds each named field for the body
    else @print("unreachable\n"),
}

The test is decided at compile time: a pattern naming a different struct never matches, so that arm is skipped and control falls to the next arm (or else). A subject that is not a struct cannot be tested this way — narrow it with as first.

Block arms in match:

var msg is match color {
    # semicolons can be used to represent line breaks
    .Red then { @print("stop\n"); "red"}
    .Green then { @print("go\n"); "green"
    else { @print("caution\n"); "yellowish"}
}

Notes:

  • Narrowing: a single-pattern arm narrows the subject to the member that arm selected, so its fields, arithmetic and later casts read as that member — the same contract as gives its branches. The subject may be a variable or a struct field (match h.val { int then h.val + 1, … }). An else arm narrows nothing (any member may have arrived) and an arm listing several patterns is not narrowed (any of them could have selected it).
  • Exhaustiveness: A match on an enum or a group covers every variant or member, or ends in else (E1033). A match on a union whose value is used covers every member or ends in else, since an uncovered member would leave it without a value; as a statement, it may cover only the members it needs.
  • Result type: All arms must produce a compatible result type. For block arms, the last expression is the arm's value.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
• if: then required else optional. Inline expressions, blocks with lift, or a bare return/break/continue.
  • as: else required then optional. Type narrowing in both branches. Blocks use lift or diverge; a bare control statement is shorthand for a diverging block.
  • match: pattern then BODY else BODY. Block arms use implicit last expression.
  • lift: provides a value from a block, terminates the block. Scopes to the immediately enclosing { }.

docs.title: Debugging Doxa programs
docs.text: Doxa writes standard debug information and leaves debugging to the tools you already have. It ships no debugger of its own.

docs.title: Building with debug info
docs.text:
Every run and compile carries debug information unless you pass --strip:

doxa compile main.doxa -o bin/main          # with debug info
doxa compile --strip main.doxa -o bin/main  # without

The debug information is a line table for every .doxa file the program was built from, with its functions, locals and types. Where it lives depends on the platform:

  • Windows: a .pdb beside the binary (bin/main.pdb).
  • Linux: a .debug file beside the binary (bin/main.debug), which the binary names in a .gnu_debuglink section. gdb, lldb and perf find it there; ship the binary alone, and keep the .debug file to debug crashes from it. Both carry the same build ID, a hash of the program, which debuginfod servers and .build-id/ debug directories index by.
  • macOS: in the object files in the compiler's cache, which the binary points to, and, for doxa compile when dsymutil is installed (it comes with Xcode's command-line tools), in a .dSYM beside the binary (bin/main.dSYM), which lldb, Instruments and crash reporters find by the binary's UUID on any machine. A fault's backtrace reads only the cache's objects, so a binary moved to another machine, or run after its cache is cleared, prints its fault line without one. (TODO: read the .dSYM too, once Zig's reader can.)

It costs the program nothing: the machine code is the same with and without it, but for the start-up that turns backtraces on. Nor does it cost measurable compile time. --strip leaves no debug information at all, the runtime's and libc's included, and no faults' backtraces: on Linux that is most of a binary's size.

What a debugger sees:

  • Functions under the names the program gives them: scale, or Point.norm for a method. DWARF also records each one's mangled link name (__doxa_m1_…) as its linkage name.
  • Lines and columns. A step moves one statement at a time and stops at the statement's start, such as the if of if x > k. A crash, a breakpoint or a profiler sample inside a statement is attributed to the expression that was running.
  • Locals, parameters and globals under the names the program spells: a var, a parameter, this, a ^ parameter, a binding an as or a match arm declares, and a module-level global. A local lent as ^, and a string variable, are read from their storage; every other is named where it is defined, so an assignment inside a branch shows the value it holds there.
  • Types. int, float and byte are their scalar types; tetra and every enum are enumerations of their values; a string value is its pointer and length, and a string variable's storage adds cap, the bytes its buffer can hold before it moves (strings); a struct is its fields, each at the offset the runtime lays it at; a union or group is its box. A fixed array expands element by element. A dynamic array points at its header: len is its length and data points at its elements, so view data as an array of len to browse them. A function value is a pointer to its signature, and each function's own signature is described.
  • Optimized builds (--opt=1..3) keep what survives optimization. That is the usual optimized-debugging experience: a statement the optimizer merged away has no stop of its own, and a value it folded away has no name.

docs.title: Backtraces on fault
docs.text:
A program follows a runtime fault's line with the Doxa frames that led to it, innermost first:

Index out of bounds at b.doxa:2:12: index 7, length 3
  in get at b.doxa:2:12
  in outer at b.doxa:6:5
  in main at b.doxa:11:5

Each frame is named as the program spells it, at the line and column of its call. The runtime's own frames are left out, and so is the call into the entry function. A fault while a global's initializer runs shows that initializer as <globals>. Optimized builds keep the frames that survive inlining. On Windows an inlined function still shows a frame of its own, though CodeView often records no column there (b.doxa:2:0); on Linux and macOS its code is shown under the function it was inlined into, at its own line. The trace goes to stderr and doesn't change the exit status. Under --strip the fault prints its line alone.

A trace shows at most 64 frames. A run of one frame, as deep recursion makes, prints once and then its count, and a trace cut short says so:

Stack overflow
  in walk at t.doxa:1:61
  in walk at t.doxa:1:72
  ... the frame above 62 more times
  ... more frames not shown

When no frame can be shown, a line says why instead, such as (no backtrace: the stack could not be unwound to the faulting frame).

A trap that is not a fault is a crash: a bad access or an illegal instruction in an inline zig block, say. It prints its line and the Doxa frames that led to it, and the program ends with the platform's crash status (an access violation on Windows, a signal elsewhere), as a native program would:

Invalid memory access at address 0x10
  in main at crash.doxa:9:5

doxa run then names how the program ended, as in doxa: the program crashed: access violation (0xC0000005) or doxa: the program was stopped by signal SEGV, and exits 1. A program that exits on its own passes its status through.

docs.title: Finding the source
docs.text: Debug information names each file by its path inside the project (main.doxa, lib/util.doxa), and a standard-library file by its place in std (std//io/io.doxa). It never records a path on the machine that built it, so a binary built in one checkout debugs the same in another. Point your debugger at the project directory once: directory <project> in gdb, settings set target.source-map in lldb, or the source-file search path in Visual Studio and WinDbg. Windows tools show such a file under a drive root, as C:\main.doxa.

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text:
The same line table lets a sampling profiler (perf, ETW/WPA, VTune, Superluminal, Instruments) attribute samples to .doxa lines. Profile an optimized build (--opt=2): it measures the program you ship.

A sampler answers how long. To learn how often, instrument the build:

doxa run fib.doxa --instrument=calls
doxa report fib

==========================================
Calls
==========================================
Built at -O0.

  177   fib fib.doxa:1:10
  1 main    fib.doxa:6:23

Each function counts its own entries, hottest first. --json prints the same data for tooling. An instrumented program writes its counts when it ends: returning from the entry, at @exit, or at a fault. They go to <binary>.profdata, beside the <binary>.profmap the compiler wrote. For doxa run that is the cache, so doxa report <stem> finds both there. For doxa compile -o out/fib, it is out/, read with doxa report out/fib; a filename with an extension, such as doxa report fib.exe, is a path beside the invocation directory, just as ./fib is. A report refuses counts from another build of the program. At --opt=1 and up, an inlined function runs no entry of its own, so its calls count toward its caller. An instrumented binary is a diagnostic build: never time it.

--instrument=lines counts each statement every time it runs, listed by its start (file:line:column) and its function, hottest first. Members combine: --instrument=calls,lines reports both tables. A loop's header counts once, as the loop statement; its condition and step run with the loop and have no row of their own.

docs.title: Static findings
docs.text:
--emit-complexity asks the compiler what each loop repeats, without running anything:

doxa run loops.doxa --emit-complexity
doxa report loops

The report lists each function's deepest loop nest, every allocation or heap store made inside a loop with the arena it lands in, calls inside loops to functions that allocate or loop, in their own body or through a function they call (calls load (allocates through parse)), and copies the compiler left to a runtime check inside a loop. An allocation marked ! lands where no iteration of its loop reclaims it, such as an element pushed into an array declared outside the loop. That memory grows with the loop's iterations and is held until its arena closes. The operations are named as --emit-hir names them (array_push, str_concat). The findings are written beside the binary as <binary>.complexity and change nothing in the program. When the same build is also instrumented, one doxa report shows the counts and the findings together, and --json prints both. With --instrument=lines, each section of findings is ordered by how often its statement ran, highest first, and each row says how often ((ran 50 times)), so what cost the run most leads.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
This document specifies groups: a nominal type that merges existing enums, structs, and other groups into a single type, re-exporting their members under qualified names. A group is a named tagged union — it provides a single type arm for function signatures and APIs without creating new values.

Status: specification. Replaces the prior set design. When implemented, update syntax.md and unions.md to reference this page.

docs.title: 1. Design invariants
docs.text: Rule Meaning Members are existing types or other groups A group contains enums, structs, and groups declared elsewhere Group membership is flattened Transitive group members are expanded into a flat member list at the declaration site Groups do not create new values Error.IO.NotFound is the same value as IO.NotFound A type appears at most once Deduplication during flattening; reaching the same type through multiple paths is harmless Members are types, not names Two distinct types may share a bare name (fs.File.OpenError, fs.Dir.OpenError); each is named by its own path Cycles are illegal A group may not include itself directly or transitively A group is the union of its members A group value fits wherever all of its members do: in a group holding them all, and in another group with the same members

docs.title: 2.1 Group declaration
docs.text:
A group is declared with the group keyword. The body lists member types.

public group Error {
    CommonError,
    IOError,
    CompilerError,
    FileError,
}

Members are referenced by their unqualified or module-qualified name. Each member contributes its variants/fields under a qualifier — its unqualified type name.

public group Error {
    error.CommonError,
    error.IOError,
    error.CompilerError,
    structs.FileError,
}

docs.title: 2.2 Transitive groups
docs.text:
A group may include another group. All members of the included group are flattened into the declaring group.

public group CoreError {
    IOError,
    CommonError,
}

public group AppError {
    CoreError,      // flattened → IOError, CommonError
    UserCancelled,
    ConfigInvalid,
}

AppError expands to { IOError, CommonError, UserCancelled, ConfigInvalid }. There is no nesting in the expanded member list.

docs.title: 2.3 Qualified access
docs.text:
Members are accessed through the group name with the qualifier:

Error.IOError.NotFound
AppError.UserCancelled           // local variant — unqualified under the group

When a variant name is unique across all group members, it may be accessed directly:

Error.NotFound                   // OK if NotFound exists in exactly one member

When ambiguous, qualified access is required:

group G {
    A,    // enum with variant X
    B,    // enum with variant X
}
G.X                              // ERROR: ambiguous — X exists in both A and B (E1039)
G.A.X                            // OK

A member's qualifier is its bare type name, and it reaches the member only while no other member shares it. Members that share a bare name are named by their own paths, which always work:

group ZigErr { zerr.fs.File.OpenError, zerr.fs.Dir.OpenError }
ZigErr.OpenError.AccessDenied    // ERROR: two members are named OpenError (E1039)
zerr.fs.Dir.OpenError.NotDir     // OK: the member's own path

Only the variants of a group's enum members count toward Group.Variant. A struct member is a type, not a value, so a struct member sharing a variant's name makes nothing ambiguous.

The same spellings name members in a match pattern: Error.IOError.NotFound then, or Error.NotFound then when NotFound is unique. A group declared in another module is reached through it, like any type: errs.Error.NotFound.

docs.title: 3.1 A union of its members
docs.text: A group names the union of its flattened members; the name adds no identity of its own. A group value is assignable wherever every one of its members is: to a group that holds them all (CoreError into AppError, which includes it), and to another group with the same members. A member type is not the group: IOError widens to AppError, and narrows back only explicitly.

docs.title: 3.2 Member identity preserved
docs.text:
A value's identity is determined by its source type — not by the group that wraps it. Error.IOError.NotFound and IOError.NotFound are the same value, of the same type: a group creates no values, so spelling a variant through the group names the member's value and types it as the member. It widens to the group wherever one is expected.

Expression Type Identity IOError.NotFound IOError IOError::NotFound Error.IOError.NotFound IOError IOError::NotFound (same) Error.NotFound (unique in Error) IOError IOError::NotFound (same) const e :: Error is IOError.NotFound Error IOError::NotFound (same)

docs.title: 3.3 Widening and narrowing
docs.text:
Widening (implicit): A value of a member type is assignable where the group type is expected, and so is a value of a group whose members the target holds (3.1). The compiler inserts a tag to track which member the value belongs to at runtime, and re-indexes it for the target group.

function open(path: string) -> string | Error {
    if path is "" then return IOError.NotFound  // widens to Error
    if path is "/" then return FileError { path } // widens to Error
    return "ok"
}

Narrowing (explicit): From a group type to a member type via match or as:

x as IOError          // succeeds if x is an IOError member; else the `else` branch runs

No implicit narrowing from a group type to a member type.

docs.title: 3.4 Equality
docs.text:
Values compare equal when they carry the same source type and same payload. A group value compares with a value of one of its members; a group-qualified variant is such a value (3.2).

Error.IOError.NotFound == IOError.NotFound     → true
e == Error.IOError.NotFound  (e :: Error)      → true when e holds IOError.NotFound
IOError.NotFound == FileError { path: "x" }    → type error (different members)

Cross-member equality is a compile error, not false.

docs.title: 3.5 Unions
docs.text:
A single group member replaces multiple individual arms in return types:

// Before
function read() -> string | IOError | CommonError | CompilerError

// After
function read() -> string | Error

A function declared returns string | Error accepts string, any Error value, or any value of a member type (widened to Error).

A union holds a group's members, not the group: string | Error is the same type as string | IOError | CommonError | CompilerError. A value keeps the member it is through the union and back — narrowing to Error with as or match gives the same Error value that went in, and Error then is a test that the union holds any of Error's members. Diagnostics and ? still name the group as written (string | >Error).

docs.title: 4.1 Exhaustiveness
docs.text:
Matching on a group must cover every member. This is a flat check over the expanded member list.

group Error { IOError, CommonError, FileError }

match err {
    IOError.NotFound then { }
    IOError.PermissionDenied then { }
    // IOError.EOF missing → not exhaustive
    CommonError.* then { }       # wildcard covers all CommonError variants
    FileError { path } then { }
}

An exhaustive match requires either: - a pattern for every variant in every enum member, plus every struct member, or - a * wildcard for any remaining enum members, or - an else arm

docs.title: 4.2 Enum patterns
docs.text:
match err {
    Error.IOError.NotFound then { }      # single variant
    Error.IOError.* then handle_io(err), # all IOError variants (narrows to IOError)
    else { }
}

Inside Error.IOError.*, the bound value is narrowed to IOError.

docs.title: 4.3 Struct patterns
docs.text:
Struct members are matched with destructuring syntax:

match err {
    Error.FileError { path } then print(path),
    Error.ConfigError { key, value } then { }
}

The struct is narrowed to its member type, and fields are available directly.

docs.title: 4.4 Matching on unions containing groups
docs.text:
match result {
    string then use(result),
    Error then handle(result),      # catch-all for the group
    Error.IOError.* then { }
}

docs.title: 5. Collisions and ill-formed programs
docs.text: Situation Verdict Two members with the same bare name after flattening Allowed; the bare name reaches neither through the group (E1039 where it is written), and a non-exhaustive match names each by its module Unqualified variant name exists in more than one member Error (ambiguous access, E1039) Cycle in group membership Error Empty group (no members) Error Group member is not a declared type Error

docs.title: 6. Runtime representation
docs.text:
A group value has a hidden tag to identify which member it belongs to, followed by the member's payload.

Group value = [member_index: u32] [payload: union { enum_variant, struct_instance }]

This is identical in shape to how tagged unions already work. The difference is that group members are named and traceable, whereas union arms are anonymous. A group value stored in a union is re-indexed to the union's position for the same member, and back when it is narrowed to the group, so the index always names a concrete member type.

The member index is stable for the lifetime of the group declaration. Reordering members changes the index and is an ABI break.

docs.title: 7. Grammar sketch
docs.text:
GroupDecl       := 'group' IDENT '{' GroupBody '}'
GroupBody       := ( GroupMember )*
GroupMember     := TypePath  (',' | NEWLINE)*
TypePath        := IDENT ( '.' IDENT )*

docs.title: 8. Differences from the prior set design
docs.text: Aspect set (old) group (new) Members Enums only Enums, structs, other groups Local variants Supported Not supported — everything is a member type Transitivity Nested qualifier chains (AppErr.Std.IO.NotFound) Flattened (AppError.IOError.NotFound) Duplicate types Error Deduplicated silently Runtime shape Enum discriminant only (zero-cost widen) Tag + payload (tagged union) is_set flag Unused Not needed — flattened at parse/semantic time
