docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
The standard library is imported like any other module. @std() is its specifier, the string "std//std.doxa" (the file std.doxa under the std root; see Modules). 

module std from @std()

docs.title: Zig errors
docs.text:
std.zerr.ZigError is an ordinary enum holding every error name in the bundled Zig standard library. It is opt-in:

import zerr from @std()

const e is zerr.ZigError.AccessDenied

Like any enum, a match on it needs an else (or every variant). The enum is generated from the bundled Zig sources by zig build zerr; zig build test runs check zerr and fails when the committed std/zerr/zerr.doxa is stale.

A std function that can fail returns T | zerr.ZigError, the error named as Zig names it (ZigError.FileNotFound, ZigError.AccessDenied). Nothing maps Zig's errors onto a coarser enum. zerr.StdError is an ordinary group of ZigError and Doxa's own runtime errors, error.Method, for code that handles both:

import zerr, error from @std()

function describe(e :: zerr.StdError) {
    match e {
        zerr.ZigError then @print("Zig: {e}\n"),
        error.Method then @print("Doxa: {e}\n"),
    }
}

No std function reports a result through state a later call reads: a second result is a struct field, and an error is the returned union.

docs.title: Build
docs.text: std.build drives the compiler from a build script. execute(c) compiles every artifact in a Context and ends the script: it exits 0 when all compile, with the compiler's status when one fails, and with 1 (after printing why) when the compiler could not run or ended by a signal. run(c) does the same work and returns the result instead, as process.Term | zerr.ZigError: how the first failing compile ended, or the last one. A cross target with no OS is ZigError.MissingOperatingSystem.

docs.title: File
docs.text: std.file reads, writes and lists files and directories relative to the working directory. A failing call returns zerr.ZigError, named as Zig names it: FileNotFound, PathAlreadyExists, NotDir, DirNotEmpty (deleting a non-empty directory without recursive), AccessDenied. An empty path is BadPathName. isDir, isFile and isPresent answer a question and never fail.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
std.http provides a buffered client plus the loopback socket primitives that the sequential server layer builds on.

module std from @std()

function printResponse(response :: Response) {
    @print("status {response.statusCode()}\n")
    @print("{response.body()}\n")
    const content_types is response.header("content-type")
    if @length(content_types) > 0 then {
        @print("content type {content_types[0]}\n")
    }
}

const response is std.http.get("https://example.com/")
response as Response then {
    const value is response
    printResponse(value)
}
else {
    @print("request failed\n")
}
  • get(url) returns Response | zerr.ZigError. HTTP status is data; a 404 still returns a response, and getText(url) returns the body regardless of status. A request that gets no response fails with the name Zig's client gives it: ConnectionRefused, UnknownHostName, Timeout when the deadline passes, HttpConnectionClosing when the server closes without answering, TooManyHttpRedirects, HttpHeadersInvalid for a header line that could break framing.
  • Request.new() creates request settings with an empty headers array and defaults of a 30-second response-read timeout and three followed redirects. Each header entry is a "Name: value" string. Set body, timeout_ms, or max_redirects on the request before calling Response.send(method, url, req). post(url, ^req), put(url, ^req), delete(url, ^req), and head(url, ^req) are thin method-specific wrappers over it.

var req is std.http.Request.new()
req.body is "hello"
@push(req.headers, "Content-Type: text/plain")
@push(req.headers, "X-Trace: demo")
const response is std.http.post("https://example.com/submit", ^req)
- Response.statusCode(), body(), header(name), and hasHeader(name) are accessors. header returns every matching value in order and compares names case-insensitively. - timeout_ms and getWithTimeout(url, timeout_ms) bound the whole exchange: name resolution, connecting, the TLS handshake, sending, and receiving. A value of 0 disables the deadline. - Redirects are followed up to max_redirects times (three by default); an exhausted limit is ZigError.TooManyHttpRedirects. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, and Cookie2 are stripped when the redirect changes the strict origin (scheme, host, or effective port). Other custom headers continue to the destination. - The server primitives bind only to loopback: listen(port) (use 0 for an ephemeral port), localAddr(listener), accept(listener), close(handle), and the request/response pair readRequest(connection) / ServerRequest.take(connection) and respond(connection, status, headers, body). readRequest is non-blocking: it returns 1 when a request is ready (read it with ServerRequest.take, a ServerRequest whose .verb, .target, and .body_text hold the parsed fields, with header(name) / hasHeader(name) reading repeated request headers case-insensitively), 0 when none has arrived yet (retry on the next Readable event), and -1 once the connection has ended; it returns int | zerr.ZigError, the error being InvalidHandle for a handle the library does not know. A malformed or oversized request never reaches the program: the library answers it (400, 413, 417, or 431) and reports the connection Closed. respond must follow a successfully parsed request (otherwise it is ZigError.NotOpenForWriting); its headers argument is a CRLF-separated blob, and the library supplies Content-Length and connection framing. A client that asks for Connection: close gets it back, and keepAlive(connection) reports whether the request may reuse the connection. accept(listener) is the low-level primitive; a poll loop reads requests from poll events instead.

  • poll(listener, timeout_ms) waits across the listener and every live connection at once and returns Event[] | zerr.ZigError (InvalidHandle for a listener that is not open). Each Event carries a connection handle and a kind :: EventKind: Accepted for a freshly accepted connection, Readable for a complete request or message waiting, and Closed once a connection has ended (closeReason(connection) says why). One poll reports a connection at most once, and keeps reporting it while messages remain unread. timeout_ms == 0 polls immediately and a negative value blocks until an event; closing the listener closes its connections and is the way to stop a loop. Connections are served by background tasks, so a slow peer never holds up another; setLimit(limit, value) adjusts the caps and deadlines (open connections, header/body/message sizes, idle and read deadlines) for connections opened afterwards. A server serves many keep-alive clients without blocking on any one connection by polling instead of calling accept directly:
const listener is std.http.listen(0) as int else 0
while true {
    const events is std.http.poll(listener, 1000) as std.http.Event[] else @panic("the listener closed")
    for i while i < @length(events) do i += 1 {
        const event is events[i]
        if event.kind == std.http.EventKind.Closed then {
            std.http.close(event.handle)
        } else {
            # 1 = request ready, 0 = wait for more bytes, -1 = ended.
            const status is std.http.readRequest(event.handle) as int else -1
            if status == 1 then {
                const value is std.http.ServerRequest.take(event.handle)
                std.http.respond(event.handle, 200, "Content-Type: text/plain\r\n", "hello {value.target}")
            } else if status < 0 then {
                std.http.close(event.handle)
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Router matches request paths to integer route ids as data: Router.new(), add(verb, pattern, id), and router.find(verb, path) → Route | nothing. A pattern segment written :name captures the matching path segment, and Route.param(name) reads the capture. Matching is exact per segment and verb, so /users/:id matches /users/42 with param("id") == "42", but not /users/42/posts or a different verb. ({} placeholders are not usable: Doxa string literals interpolate on {.)
var router is std.http.Router.new()
router.add("GET", "/users/:id", 1)

const matched is router.find("GET", "/users/42")
matched as Route then {
    const id is matched.param("id") as string else ""
    @print("user {id}\n")
}
  • download(url) / downloadUrl(url, destination) use the same redirect, timeout, and status handling as requests, but stream response bytes directly to the destination file, and return the response status as int | zerr.ZigError. A non-2xx status is the server's answer, not a failure: its body is written like any other.
  • WebSockets upgrade a connection after its handshake request has been read: isWebSocket(connection) reports whether the handshake has completed, and upgradeWebSocket(connection) completes the RFC 6455 handshake on a buffered request that asked to switch protocols. wsSend(connection, op, data) sends one frame; wsNext(connection) advances the decoder and returns 1 when a message is ready (read it with wsMessage, whose op is WsOp.Text, Binary, Ping, Pong, or Close and whose data is the payload), 0 when none is waiting (retry on the next Readable event), 2 when the peer closed, and ZigError.ProtocolError on a protocol or size violation. A frame sent to a connection that has ended is ZigError.Closed. Fragmented messages are reassembled before they are surfaced, and control frames are surfaced rather than handled silently, so the caller owns ping/pong/close policy. Frames are read in the background, so a partial frame from one peer cannot stall other connections. A WebSocket with no incoming frame for Limit.IdleMs (120 s by default) is closed as CloseReason.IdleTimeout; until heartbeats land, a peer stays open by sending something, a ping included, within it. A text message that is not valid UTF-8, a malformed close frame, or a frame larger than 16 MiB fails the connection with the corresponding Close code (1007 / 1002 / 1009).
const listener is std.http.listen(0) as int else 0
while true {
    const events is std.http.poll(listener, 1000) as std.http.Event[] else @panic("the listener closed")
    for i while i < @length(events) do i += 1 {
        const event is events[i]
        if event.kind == std.http.EventKind.Closed then {
            std.http.close(event.handle)
        } else {
            if not std.http.isWebSocket(event.handle) then {
                const status is std.http.readRequest(event.handle) as int else -1
                if status == 1 then {
                    std.http.upgradeWebSocket(event.handle)
                } else if status < 0 then {
                    std.http.close(event.handle)
                }
            }
            if std.http.isWebSocket(event.handle) then {
                var reading is true
                while reading {
                    const ws is std.http.wsNext(event.handle) as int else -1
                    if ws == 1 then {
                        const message is std.http.wsMessage(event.handle)
                        if message.op == std.http.WsOp.Text then {
                            std.http.wsSend(event.handle, std.http.WsOp.Text, message.data)
                        } else if message.op == std.http.WsOp.Close then {
                            std.http.wsSend(event.handle, std.http.WsOp.Close, message.data)
                            std.http.close(event.handle)
                            reading is false
                        }
                    } else if ws == 2 or ws < 0 then {
                        std.http.close(event.handle)
                        reading is false
                    } else {
                        reading is false
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Most servers only need the Go-flavoured sugar; the primitives above stay public for full control:

  • wsAccept(connection) completes the handshake once the request is buffered and returns true once the connection is a WebSocket (it is a no-op after). It returns false while no request has arrived. A request that is not an upgrade is answered 426 Upgrade Required.
  • wsRead(connection) returns the next Message, nothing when none is buffered yet or the peer closed, or an error on failure.
  • wsWrite(connection, op, data) sends a frame with an explicit opcode; wsText, wsBinary, wsPing, wsPong name the common kinds, and wsClose(connection) sends a Close frame and drops the connection.
const listener is std.http.listen(0) as int else 0
while true {
    const events is std.http.poll(listener, 1000)
    for i while i < @length(events) do i += 1 {
        const event is events[i]
        if event.kind == std.http.EventKind.Closed then {
            std.http.close(event.handle)
        } else if std.http.wsAccept(event.handle) then {
            var reading is true
            while reading {
                const m is std.http.wsRead(event.handle)
                m as Message then {
                    const message is m
                    if message.op == std.http.WsOp.Text then {
                        std.http.wsText(event.handle, "echo: {message.data}")
                    } else if message.op == std.http.WsOp.Close then {
                        std.http.wsClose(event.handle)
                        reading is false
                    }
                } else {
                    reading is false
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Client WebSockets (dialing out to ws:// / wss://) are not available yet; see phase R4 of plan/http-robustness.md.

docs.title: IO
docs.text:
std.io writes to standard output and standard error and reads standard input.

  • print(text) and println(text) write to standard output, eprint and eprintln to standard error; the ln forms add the platform's line ending ( on Windows). Each returns nothing | zerr.ZigError (ZigError.WriteFailed when the stream cannot be written).
  • input() returns the next line without its or , inputByte() the next byte, and inputPrompt(prompt) prints prompt and then reads a line. At the end of input each returns nothing: running out of input is an outcome, not an error. A failed read is a zerr.ZigError (ReadFailed; StreamTooLong for a line longer than the 4 KiB input buffer).
  • Every read goes through one buffered reader, so a byte read after a line sees what the line read buffered past it.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
std.json parses a document into a handle-based tree and writes one back out. A Node is a small generation-checked handle into a single document slot, so retaining one past the next parse is safe: it reads as Kind.Invalid rather than a dangling value.

module std from @std()

const result is std.json.Node.parse("{\"name\":\"doxa\",\"stars\":5}")
match result {
    std.json.Node then {
        const name is result.field("name")
        match name {
            std.json.Node then @print("{name.text()}\n")
            else @print("no name\n")
        }
    }
    else {
        @print("malformed\n")
    }
}
  • parse(text) returns Node | zerr.ZigError, the error named as Zig's JSON parser names it: SyntaxError for a malformed document, UnexpectedEndOfInput for one that stops early, DuplicateField for a repeated key. Objects keep their key order.
  • The writer refuses what that parser would reject, by the same name: a write the grammar does not allow (a value where a key was expected, an unbalanced end(), a second root value, NaN or infinity, a tetra's both or neither) is SyntaxError, and finish() with a container still open or nothing written is UnexpectedEndOfInput. Text that is not UTF-8 is InvalidUtf8.
  • kind() never fails and returns a Kind: Invalid, Null, Boolean, Integer, Number, Text, Array, or Object. An integer that the runtime could not fit in i64 or an exponent beyond the float range arrives as Number (1e400 reads as infinity from floatValue()).
  • count(), element(index), field(name), key(), text(), intValue(), floatValue(), and booleanValue() are strict: a wrong kind, a missing field, or an out-of-range index yields nothing. count works on arrays and objects; field only on objects; the value accessors only on the matching scalar kind.
  • Writing mirrors the document shape: beginObject() / beginArray() open a container, writeKey(name) precedes a member value, and end() closes it. finish() returns the escaped text as string | zerr.ZigError and releases the writer; the next writer call starts a fresh document. A refused write refuses the rest of its document, and finish() reports it; the document after it starts clean.
  • The writer emits \b, \f, \n, \r, \t as their two-character escapes and any other control byte below 0x20 as a lowercase \u00xx sequence. It validates UTF-8 before quoting and refuses NaN or infinity.

docs.title: Math
docs.text:
std.math holds the numeric limits. Each is a constant expression, so a call folds to its value. Wrapping arithmetic is the +%, -% and *% operators, not a library call (Overflow and wrapping).

module std from @std()

function inRange(x :: int, delta :: int) returns tetra {
    return delta <= 0 or x <= std.math.maxInt() - delta
}
  • Limits: maxInt() and minInt() (i64), maxByte() and minByte() (0xFF, 0x00), maxFloat() (the largest finite float), minFloat() (-maxFloat(), the lowest finite float), and minNormalFloat() (the smallest positive normal float).

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
std.process runs other programs and reads the program's own arguments and environment. Running a program comes in two forms: one passes a command line to the platform shell, the other starts a program directly with its arguments.

import process from @std()

# Portable: no shell, so the path and arguments arrive as written.
const run is process.execCaptureArgs("bin/tool", ["--version"]) as process.Run else {
    return
}
if run.term.succeeded() then @print(run.stdout)

# Shell: the command line is cmd.exe's on Windows, `sh`'s elsewhere.
const built is process.execOk("make all")
  • Shell commands. exec(command) runs command and waits for it; execCapture(command) also captures what it writes; execOk(command) says whether it ran and exited 0. The text is handed to the platform shell unchanged: cmd.exe on Windows, sh -c elsewhere. Its grammar is that shell's: quoting, pipes, %VAR% or $VAR. On Windows / begins a switch, so an unquoted relative program path must use \ (bin\tool) or be quoted ("bin/tool"); bin/tool runs bin with the switch /tool.
  • Programs. execArgs(program, arguments) runs program and waits for it; execCaptureArgs(program, arguments) also captures what it writes. No shell is involved: program is a path (/ or \ on Windows) or a name looked up on PATH, and each argument arrives as one argument. These are the form to use for a path a program computed, such as a build script running what it just compiled. execArgsEnv and execCaptureEnv take two more arrays, env_keys and env_values, set in the child's environment on top of the parent's.
  • Results. The exec forms return a Term, how the child ended: kind (TermKind.Exited, Signal, Stopped or Unknown, as Zig reports it) and code, the exit status or signal number. term.succeeded() is "exited with 0". The capture forms return a Run: its term, and the child's stdout and stderr. A non-zero exit is part of the result, not an error.
  • Failures are zerr.ZigError values, named as Zig names them: a program that does not exist is ZigError.FileNotFound, one that cannot run ZigError.InvalidExe or ZigError.AccessDenied. A failure means the program never ran (or could not be waited for); nothing of the result is built.
  • The program itself. args() returns every argument, the program's own path first; argc() is how many, and argv(index) one of them, or error.Method.OutOfBounds. cwd() is the working directory (or a ZigError). getenv(name) is an environment variable as the program started with it, or nothing when it is not set. exit(code) ends the program with code; a POSIX parent sees its low byte.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Doxa strings are UTF-8 encoded and backed by a contiguous u8 buffer. The byte length is explicit: it is not inferred from a terminating NUL, and embedded U+0000 bytes are valid. Inside Zig, values are []const u8 slices; at the inline Zig module boundary they cross as pointer + byte length (a (ptr, u64 len) parameter pair, or out_ptr/out_len out-params for returns), as documented in zig.md.

Every runtime string helper takes pointer + length and never reads past the length; no string is NUL-terminated. Byte lengths at that compiled boundary are a fixed 64-bit u64 on every target (matching the emitted IR's i64 lengths); only pointers follow the target's pointer width.

docs.title: Quote semantics
docs.text:
Double-quoted strings ("...") interpret {expression} blocks anywhere in the string body. Any valid Doxa expression — a variable, an arithmetic operation, a function call — can appear between the braces and will be stringified in place at runtime:

var name is "Doxa"
@print("Hello {name}!\n")

var x is 10
@print("{x} squared is {x ** 2}\n")

A placeholder holds exactly one expression: "{x y}" is an error at the y (E2023), never "{x}" with the rest dropped.

Interpolation works wherever a string literal is accepted: in @print / @println calls, variable initialisers, function arguments, and so on. A module path and a match pattern are constants, so a string there holds no placeholder.

docs.title: Escapes
docs.text:
A backslash starts an escape. These are all of them:

Escape Means " a double quote \ a backslash a line feed a carriage return a tab \{, \} a literal brace, never a placeholder \u{...} the code point with 1–6 hex digits, as UTF-8

Any other escape is an error. A brace an escape produces is text: "\u{7b}" is {. An unescaped { always opens a placeholder, which closes on its line (or on a line it continues with ...), so "a{b" is an error that says to write "a\{b". A placeholder's source is code: a string inside it has its own escapes and placeholders ("{"q"}"}" is q"}).

A raw line break inside a literal is one byte of the string, , unless the next line begins with ..., which continues the literal without it. A file with Windows line endings ( ) means the same program: each line break is still .

docs.title: The string type
docs.text:
string is a first-class primitive type alongside int, float, byte, tetra, and nothing:

var s :: string is "hello"               # explicit type annotation
var t is "world"                         # inferred as string

A string variable always holds a value — there is no null/nil sentinel. The empty string is represented by "".

docs.title: Values and variables
docs.text:
A string is a value: storing one never lets two names see each other's changes. Underneath, a string value is a pointer and a byte length, and its bytes are never rewritten once written, so a store, an argument or a struct field shares them rather than copying.

A string variable — a var, a parameter, a module-level var — is a buffer: its value plus room to grow. Appending to it writes into that room, and when the room runs out the variable moves to a buffer twice the size. Building a string in a loop therefore costs time and memory in proportion to its length:

var out is ""
each word in words {
    @push(out, word)        # also: out += word, out is out + word, out is "{out}{word}"
}

Reading part of a string allocates nothing: @slice, s[i], each c in s, @pop, and @remove of the first or last byte are views of the bytes already there. A template or a chain of + builds its result with one allocation, numbers written straight into it. @pack of a fresh byte array (a literal, a call's result) keeps the array's bytes; of an array a variable holds, it copies them, since the variable could still write them.

A value taken from the variable before an append keeps what it held. A string in a struct field or an array element is a value, not a variable: appending to one builds a new string, so build text in a variable and store it once. s[i] is x is an error on purpose — rewriting a byte would make every string store a copy.

docs.title: Underlying u8 array
docs.text:
Strings are stored as an array of unsigned 8-bit bytes. This means you can bridge between strings and byte data with pack and unpack:

Builtin Signature Description @pack(bytes) byte[] → string Interpret each byte as a u8 codepoint @unpack(string) string → byte[] Decompose a string into byte values 
const bytes :: byte[] is [0x48, 0x69, 0x21]   # [72, 105, 33]
const word is @pack(bytes)                     # "Hi!"
const back is @unpack(word)                    # byte[] is [72, 105, 33]

@pack requires a byte[]; an array of integer literals narrows to byte in the same way as any other byte context. @unpack decomposes a string byte-for-byte, so @pack / @unpack round-trip the underlying u8 storage.

docs.title: Common operations
docs.text:
Expression Result "abc" + "def" "abcdef" length("hello") 5 "hello"[0] "h" (a 1-byte string) "こんにちは"[0] the leading byte of the first character, as a string string(42) "42" string(3.14) "3.14" type("hello") "string"

A string and a byte[] do not share elements. Indexing, @pop, @remove, and @slice on a string produce strings; the same operations on a byte[] produce bytes. @pack and @unpack are the only bridge between the two.

Indexing, slicing, @find, @pop, @remove, and for/each iteration all address bytes, not UTF-8 codepoints — @length is the byte length — so "こんにちは"[0] is the leading byte of a three-byte character, not the whole character, and each c in "日本語" yields nine one-byte strings. To walk codepoints, @unpack the string and reconstruct with @pack, or use a Zig block for Unicode-aware processing.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
== and != compare strings byte for byte. <, <=, > and >= order them lexicographically by byte: the first differing byte decides, and a string sorts before any longer string it is a prefix of.

"apple" < "banana"   # true
"app" < "apple"      # true
"Z" < "a"            # true — uppercase ASCII sorts before lowercase
"z" < "é"            # true

For UTF-8 this is exactly Unicode code-point order, so it is total, locale-free and stable across platforms. It is not a collation: it knows nothing of case folding or accents. Locale-aware ordering belongs in a library, not an operator.

docs.title: Interop with Zig
docs.text:
For inline Zig modules (zig { … } blocks compiled into the program), the generated wrappers pass strings as pointer + byte length, not C strings. See zig.md for the full ABI.

A string variable crosses as the value it holds: a Zig function never sees a buffer's spare room.

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Since Doxa has a tightly limited number of types, structs are useful for modeling more complex data. Structs are based off composition to avoid pitfalls inherent to inheretance. Fields, functions, and methods are all private unless marked public.

Struct instantiation always requires a $ sigil prefix. An identifier followed by { without $ is always parsed as an implicit match expression — never as a struct literal.

docs.title: Real world example
docs.text:
struct Point {
    x :: int, # unless marked public, fields are private
    y :: int,

    public id :: int,

    public function New(x :: int, y :: int) returns Point { # functions are static
        return $Point { # note the $ prefix
            x is x,
            y is y,
            id is 0,
        }
    }

    function safeSub(a :: int, b :: int) returns int { # private: callable only inside Point
        const result is a - b
        if result > 255 or result < 0 then return -1
        return result
    }

    public method getDelta() returns int { # a method has a receiver, `this`
        return Point.safeSub(this.x, this.y)
    }
}

const p is Point.New(5, 2)
p.getDelta()? # 3

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
A private member belongs to its struct alone:

  • A private field is read and written only through this (this.x), so only in the struct's own methods.
  • A private method is called only through this (this.reset()).
  • A private function is called through this or through the type (Point.safeSub(...)) from inside the struct.
  • A struct literal may set a private field only inside the struct, so a struct with private fields is built by its own functions.

Nothing else reaches a private member — not other structs in the same file, and not module-level functions. A struct's function has no this; only a method does.

docs.title: Basic Composition Example
docs.text:
struct Animal {
    public name :: string,
}

struct Dog {
    # Composition instead of inheritance
    animal :: Animal,
    breed :: string,

    public function new(name :: string, breed :: string) returns Dog {
        return $Dog {
            animal is $Animal { name is name },
            breed is breed,
        }
    }

    public method bark() {
        @print("{this.animal.name} says woof!\n")
    }
}

const dog is Dog.new("Spot", "Labrador")
dog.bark() # Spot says woof!

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Structs are allocated from the current scope's arena. All field values are stored in a single contiguous pool alongside field metadata, giving excellent cache locality. Assigning a struct held by another name copies it, so a write through one name is never seen through the other; a fresh struct (a $ literal, a call's result) is moved, not copied. Sharing is written with ^ (see alias.md). ```

docs.title: Core Language Features
docs.text: A source file is UTF-8. A byte order mark at its very start is ignored; one anywhere else is an error.

docs.title: Primitive Types
docs.text: Doxa has two general categories of types, scalar and composite:

docs.title: Scalar
docs.text:
Scalar types are the most basic units of data. Currently Doxa has 3 default number types. Types listed reflect their Zig equivilent. Bigint may be added in the future for increased flexibility.

int (64 bit integer) float (64 bit floating point) byte (8 bit hex literal) string tetra (2 bit integer) enum nothing (void)

int and byte arithmetic never wraps silently. A byte is unsigned, so 0xFF + 0x01 and 0x00 - 0x01 fault, like int overflow, in every build mode; +%, -% and *% wrap modulo 256 on request (Overflow and wrapping).

docs.title: Composite
docs.text:
Composite types are constructed out of scalar types. They are

array - must be homogenous struct - no classes, no inheretance, only composition group - can be used as an umbrella type for enums and structs union - can be handled with switch statements and type narrowing, see page on unions for more info

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
A name has one meaning wherever it can be seen. Doxa has no shadowing and no overloading:

  • A declaration inside a function, a block, a loop or a pattern may not reuse a name already visible where it appears: an enclosing local or parameter, or any top-level name of the file. A file's top-level names are visible throughout it, so a parameter may not share a name with a global declared further down (E1035).
  • A file binds each top-level name once, whether by a declaration, a module alias, an import, or a zig block (E1002). Two imports of symbols that share a name conflict; import one through a module alias instead (Modules).
  • A struct names each member once: no two fields, no two methods or functions, and no method or function sharing a field's name (E1002).
  • Functions and types are declared at file scope only (E2029), so a function never hides another inside a body.
  • Expressions, blocks and type expressions nest at most 256 deep (E2031).
  • Only an identifier names a declaration: a function, parameter, method, variable, field, type, enum variant or loop variable. A keyword (to, at, exists, …) is refused where it is declared (E2032), since no expression could refer to it.

A binding that is not visible does not conflict, so sibling blocks may each declare the same name:

{
    var t :: int is 1
}
{
    var t :: string is "two"   # fine: the first `t` is out of scope
}

Narrowing does not declare anything: inside x as int then { … } or a match arm, x is the same variable seen at a narrower type. Likewise, inside the branches of const v is expr as T else { … }, v is the declaration itself, holding the subject narrowed to that branch's type.

docs.title: Line Continuation
docs.text:
A newline ends a statement. A statement, a declaration or a return holds one expression, and must end where that expression does: const y is 5 6 is an error at the 6 (E2023). A statement that computes a value and drops it, such as a bare x + 1, does nothing and is a warning (W2012). To continue one expression across lines, begin the next line with ..., which joins it to the line above:

function inRange(v :: int) returns tetra {
    return v >= 0
        ...and v <= 7
}

... must be the first thing on its line. Placed anywhere else it is an error:

return @length("ab") == 2 ...and true
                          ^^^ EllipsisWithoutNewline: '...' continuation must follow a completed line

docs.title: Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
Arithmetic follows Python-like semantics. See the Arithmetic page for full details on type promotion, division, and modulo.

Operator Name Example + Addition 1 + 2 → 3 - Subtraction 3 - 1 → 2 * Multiplication 2 * 3 → 6 ** Exponentiation 2 ** 3 → 8 / Float division 10 / 4 → 2.5 // Integer division (floored) -7 // 2 → -4 % Modulo (floored) -7 % 2 → 1

Compound assignment is supported for all arithmetic operators: +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **=.

target op= value computes its target's place once: in a[k()] += 1, k() runs once, and the element it reads is the one it writes.

//= and %= are integer-only, matching their binary forms: both operands must be int or byte.

/= is the exception that looks like the others but is not. Doxa's / is float division, so /= computes a float whatever the operands are — assigning that back into an int is a narrowing, which Doxa rejects everywhere else. Use //= for integer division:

var n is 10
n /= 3      # Error: Float is not assignable to type Int
n //= 3     # n is now 3

var f is 10.0
f /= 4      # f is now 2.5

Dividing or taking a remainder by zero is a runtime fault (Division by zero at <file>:<line>:<column>, exit 1; see Runtime faults) rather than undefined behaviour. Float division is unaffected and follows IEEE 754, so 5 / 0 is inf.

docs.title: Comparison Operators
docs.text:
==, !=, <, <=, > and >= compare two numbers or two strings. Two tetras, two values of the same enum, or two nothings compare with == and != only. A group value compares through the member it holds, so err == IOError.Denied tests an error set against one of its members. Anything else — structs, arrays, functions, values of two different enums, an ordering of tetras or enums, or a union value — is a compile error (E1016). A union must be narrowed first:

var u :: int | string is 3
const three is u as int then u == 3 else false

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Double-quoted strings interpolate expressions in {...} anywhere a string expression is accepted:

var name is "Doxa"
var greeting is "Hello {name}"
@print("{greeting}\n")

A literal brace is written \{ or \}. The escapes are \", \\, \n, \r, \t, \{, \} and \u{...}; see strings.md.

The tetra type represents a four cornered value with the possible states: true, false, both, and neither. For additional information see the tetra page.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays are homogeneous collections with type inference:

var nums :: int[] is [1, 2, 3]    # Explicit typing
var strs is ["a", "b"]            # Inferred as string[]

# Invalid operations
var mixed is [1, "two", true]     # Error: mixed types
@push(nums, "four")                # Error: type mismatch

docs.title: Array Storage Kinds
docs.text:
Doxa tracks how every array is stored, and that storage kind determines which builtins can mutate it.

  • dynamic — default for var arrays and anything returned from runtime helpers. These can grow and shrink freely.
  • fixed — any type annotation that names a literal size (for example, int[4]) produces a fixed array. Type aliases preserve this metadata, so wrapping int[4] in an alias and then declaring var data :: MyAlias still behaves as fixed storage with an immutable length/capacity.
  • const literal — a const binding that receives a compile-time literal (including nested literals) is tagged immutable. Any other const that aliases that value inherits the same storage kind.

Mutating methods like @push, @insert, @remove, or @clear require dynamic storage. Coerce a fixed/const literal array into dynamic form by copying it into a mutable declaration:

const literal = [1, 2]
var copy :: int[] is literal  # copy becomes dynamic and @push-friendly
````

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text:
```doxa enum Status { Success, Error, Pending }

var result is match status { .Success => "all good", .Error => "failed", else => "waiting" } ```

Match expressions must be exhaustive or include an else clause.

docs.title: Enum variant shorthand
docs.text:
.Variant names a variant of the enum its position expects, and nothing else gives it a type. The context must be explicit: a parameter, an annotated or already-declared variable, a struct field, an annotated array, a return, or the other side of a comparison.

```doxa var status :: Status is .Pending # annotation status is .Success # declared variable if status == .Error then { … } # comparison report(.Error) # parameter

const bad is .Success # error: no context; write Status.Success ```

A shorthand the expected enum does not declare is an error naming the enum.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Errors are best handled with custom enum and type unions.

```doxa enum Error { TOO_BIG, TOO_SMALL, }

const res is intOrError() res as int then { intsOnly(res) # narrowed to int } else { match res { # else blocks do not narrow Error.TOO_BIG then { @print("result was too big") } Error.TOO_SMALL then { @print("result was too small") } else { # we know this will never be reached unreachable } } }

```

docs.title: unreachable
docs.text: Use the unreachable keyword when a control-flow path should be impossible. It behaves like Zig's unreachable: the compiler treats it as a no-return expression for type checking and reaching it at runtime is a fault: Reached unreachable code at <file>:<line>:<column>, exit 2 (see Runtime faults).

docs.title: Peek operator (?)
docs.text:
Evaluates the operand for its side effect only: it prints a debug line (file/line/column when available, variable name, static type, and runtime value) and leaves the value on the stack unchanged. Output goes through Zig’s std.debug.print (typically stderr), so it stays separate from normal stdout (@print, std.io.print, and so on) and does not use the same fallible stdout path.

doxa var x is computeValue() x? # Prints value with location, name, and type [./test.doxa:2:2] x :: int is 62

docs.title: Range (to)
docs.text:
Ranges are arrays which can be declared between two ints or bytes

const range is 10 to 15 @print("{range}") # [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]

docs.title: Collection Quantifiers
docs.text:
As with all formal logic operations, both symbolic notation and keyword notations are supported.

doxa (∃x ∈ numbers : x > 10) # Logical notation (exists x in numbers where x > 10) # English prose (∀x ∈ numbers : x > 0) # Logical notation (forall x in numbers where x > 0) # English prose

docs.title: Conditional Expressions
docs.text:
All conditionals can be used as expressions to assign values:

doxa var result is if condition then { value1 } else { value2 }

Be aware assigning an expression without a value will assign nothing: doxa var x is if (false) { y is 1 } # x becomes nothing

docs.title: Function Return Types
docs.text:
Functions can specify return types using the returns syntax. Any type can be returned, including composite types, but only one type at a time. This is one of the places where type unions can come in handy.

doxa function add(a :: int, b :: int) returns int { return a + b }

A function that declares returns returns on every path: no path may reach the end of its body (E5011). Reaching the end is a bare return, so a function whose return type includes nothing may let a path reach it, and returns nothing there. A path ends at a return, unreachable, @panic or @exit, at an if or as whose branches all end, at a match that covers its subject and whose arms all end, or at a loop that nothing but a break could stop and that holds none.

A function or method without returns returns nothing. It may return early, but returning a value from it is an error:

```doxa function log(message :: string) { if message == "" then return # fine: returns nothing @print(message) }

function add(a :: int, b :: int) { return a + b # error: 'add' declares no returns, so it cannot return a value } ```

The converse holds too: a bare return returns nothing, so a function that declares returns may use one only when its return type includes nothing. A function returns exactly what it declares; nothing widens the type for it.

```doxa function check(n :: int) returns nothing | Error { if n > 0 then return # fine: the declared type includes nothing return IOError.Denied }

function strict(n :: int) returns Error { if n > 0 then return # error: 'strict' returns Error, so a bare return has no value to give return IOError.Denied } ```

docs.title: First order logic
docs.text:
First order logic always produces a true or false value. For more information on tetras see the tetra page.

Doxa has extensive for traditional first order logics that work as expected with true and false values. These can be represented in formal unicode notation:

``` const arr :: int[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

docs.title: existential quantifier ∃, element of ∈
docs.text: ∃x ∈ arr : x > 3 # true

docs.title: universal quantifier ∀, where :
docs.text: ∀x ∈ arr : x > 3 # false

docs.title: NOT ¬
docs.text: ¬false # true

docs.title: biconditional ↔
docs.text: false ↔ false # true

docs.title: XOR ⊕
docs.text: true ⊕ true # false

docs.title: AND ∧
docs.text: true ∧ false # false

docs.title: OR ∨
docs.text: true ∨ false # true

docs.title: NAND ↑
docs.text: true ↑ false # true

docs.title: NOR ↓
docs.text: true ↓ false # false

docs.title: implication →
docs.text:
true → false # false ```

This unicode support is paired with plaintext keywords which act in an identical fashion:

∃ - exists ∀ - forall ∈ - in : - where ¬ - not (`!` is also accepted) ↔ - iff ⊕ - xor ∧ - and ∨ - or ↑ - nand ↓ - nor → - implies

This means formal logical representation can be written in either way:

``` const arr :: int[] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

¬(∀x ∈ arr : x > 3) # true not (forall x in arr where x > 3) # true ```

docs.title: Paradoxical logic
docs.text:
Every binary tetra operator reads whether each operand holds (true and both hold, false and neither do not) and answers true or false; not is the one operator that keeps a contradiction. The rule is in Tetras, "Intentionality". For and (rows are the left operand) and not:

and T F B N T T F T F F F F F F B T F T F N F F F F not T F F T B B N N

docs.title: Type overview
docs.text:
A tetra is a type which tries to represent four cornered logic rather than traditional binary logic. You can think of a tetra a like an extended boolean type. In its simplest sense, where bools can exist in only two states, true or false, tetras can exist in four:

true - These first two values should be familiar false both - This is equivalent to both true and false neither - This is equivalent neither to true or false

docs.title: An Example
docs.text:
Let's start with a condition, in this case, the condition of being alive. In traditional boolean logic there would be only two states for this condition, true or false, alive or dead. But a tetra can represent logical conditions outside of this true/false, alive/dead binary.

Here are four values to represent the four possible states or corners of a tetra:

const Bob is true
const Shakespeare is false
const zombie is both
const angel is neither

Now let's create some conditional logic to understand how a tetra works. Here is a function to discover whether something is alive or not. It takes a single tetra for input then decides if something is alive or not based on whether it is true or false. it then compares the two flags, isAlive and isDead in order to determine the state.

function living(alive :: tetra) returns string {
    var isAlive is false
    var isDead is false

    if alive then isAlive is true
    if not alive then isDead is true

    if isAlive and isDead then return "is alive and dead"
    if isAlive then return "is alive"
    if isDead then return "is dead"
    return "neither alive or dead"
}

You might notice this function could be written without the flags, by comparing the state of the tetra itself. We are using flags here to deconstruct it in a way we might parse this to using traditional boolean logic. Here is an execution of the function:

@print("Bob {living(Bob)}\n")
@print("Shakespeare {living(Shakespeare)}\n")
@print("zombie {living(zombie)}\n")
@print("angel {living(angel)}\n")

And here is the output I received:

Bob is alive
Shakespeare is dead
zombie is alive and dead
angel neither alive or dead

When deconstructed like this we can see the logic is relatively simple. True only triggers conditions which are true. False only triggers conditions which are false. Both will always trigger a condition. Neither will never trigger a condition.

A purely functional way to imagine this is that both is a true value which cannot be negated, and neither is a false value which cannot be negated.

Keep in mind, a tetra is a value just like a boolean is. A tetra doesn't alter the flow of conditional branches, rather it provides states which trigger conditionals in a paradoxical way.

We treat the else clause as exactly what it sounds like: "if a condition is met, then do x, or else do y". Since both will always trigger a condition, and neither will never trigger a condition, both will never trigger the else clause, and neither will always trigger the else clause.

docs.title: A use case
docs.text:
Where a tetra really excels is dealing with fuzzy or ambigious data. Take a common example of ambigous data, API calls. Here we are fetching data from an API whose validity we may not be sure of. The call will be stored in a struct which uses a tetra called valid:

true mean the data was valid false means the data was invalid both means the data was ambigous, possibly valid, possibly not neither means no data was returned

This approach lets us handle ambigous data without using flags or nested if statements:

struct Call {
    data :: string
    valid :: tetra
}

const result :: Call is apiCall()

if not result.valid then log(result) # if the result is not valid or ambigous it is logged 
if result.valid then serveData(result) # if the result is valid or ambigous it is served
# if no data the conditionals do not trigger and the result falls through

docs.title: Intentionality
docs.text: In order to reduce complexity adding contradition into the system must be intentional. There are two ways of adding contradition (both or neither) into the system. First, you can set a tetra manually as both or neither. Second, you can use a special operator called paradoxical and, which will take the input (true and false) as both. Other than this expect a traditional binary result (true or false). All first order logic in doxa necessarily returns a value of true or false. Each binary operator (and, or, xor, iff, nand, nor, implies) reads whether each operand holds (both does, neither does not) and returns true or false, so both and true is true and neither or false is false. not keeps a contradiction: not both is both.

docs.title: What are unions
docs.text: Unions are a special type which can represent one type or another. For instance, you can make a value that either returns a number, or a string. A union can only hold a single value, and therefore represent a single type when used.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Unions are declared using pipes:

var x :: int | float
var y :: string | int | float

The pipe's only usage in Doxa is to specify a typed union.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# A union that can be either an integer or a float
var number :: int | float
number is 42     # Valid - integer
number is 3.14   # Valid - float

# A union that can be a string, integer, or float
var value :: string | int | float
value is "hello" # Valid - string
value is 100     # Valid - integer
value is 2.718   # Valid - float

# Unions default to the first type when not initialized
var defaulted :: int | float
defaulted?       # Prints 0 (default int value)

var float_first :: float | int
float_first?     # Prints 0.0 (default float value)

docs.title: Default Behavior
docs.text:
When a union is declared without initialization, it defaults to the first type in the union with its default value:

  • int defaults to 0
  • float defaults to 0.0
  • byte defaults to 0x00
  • string defaults to ""
  • tetra defaults to false
  • nothing defaults to nothing

This ensures that unions always have a well-defined state and the compiler knows which type is currently active.

docs.title: Optional Values
docs.text:
A common use case for unions is representing optional values using nothing:

# Optional integer
var maybe_name :: string | nothing
maybe_name is "Alice"     # Has a value
maybe_name is nothing # No value

# Function that might not return a value
function findValue(arr :: MyObject[], target :: string) returns(int | nothing) {
    each x in arr {
        if (x.name equals target) then {
            return x
        }
    }
    return nothing # Not found
}

docs.title: Why unions are useful
docs.text:
Unions are particularly useful when:

  • A function can return different types depending on the input
  • A variable needs to hold different types at different times
  • You want to represent optional values (like T | nothing)
  • You're working with data that can have multiple valid representations

docs.title: Using a union value
docs.text:
A union value is usable only as the member it is holding: reading its fields, doing arithmetic on it, or passing it where a member type is expected all require it to be narrowed first — with as, or by matching it (control.md). Narrowing holds for the branch that selected the member and no further; which branches narrow is described under match.

Printing or peeking a union (or group) value shows the member it holds. An enum member is written with its type, since a union may hold variants of several enums; once narrowed, it is a plain enum again:

var u :: int | IOError is IOError.Denied
@print("{u}\n")                  # IOError.Denied
@print("{u as IOError else IOError.NotFound}\n")  # .Denied

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Here is a robust example of how error handling can be done using Doxa. Note that none of this handling is specific to errors, it is a general return pattern which relies on normal values making semanitcs extremely clear and flexible. This relies on the as keyword which attempts to narrow a value into another type.

enum ErrorList {
    Overflow,
    Underflow,
}

# Match function to process errors
function handleError(err :: ErrorList) {
    match err {
        .Overflow then doSomething(),
        .Underflow then doSomethingElse(),
    }
}

# Function returns a union - we won't know if the value is a number or one of our errors until we check
function addLimit(a :: int, b :: int) returns( int | ErrorList ) {
    const result is a + b
    if result > 255 then return ErrorList.Overflow
    if result < 0 then return ErrorList.Underflow
    return result
}

# All of these return unions
const unknownBigResult is addLimit(1000, 1000)   # ErrorList.Overflow
const unknownSmallResult is addLimit(100, -1000) # ErrorList.Underflow
const unknownRightResult is addLimit(100, -10)   # 90

# Handle errors - several approaches:

# Approach 1: Pattern matching (cleanest)
match unknownRightResult {
    int then onlyUsesInts(unknownRightResult),  # unknownRightResult is typed as int here
    ErrorList then handleError(unknownRightResult),  # unknownRightResult is typed as ErrorList here
}

# Approach 2: Explicit fallback with error handling
const myInt is unknownRightResult as int else {
    @panic("This should never happen in production!")
}
onlyUsesInts(myInt)

# Note type checking in control flow doesn't implicitly cast unlike match case which is exhaustive
# this can be done by narrowing within the branch but it is not as ergonomic as match case
if unknownRightResult @istype int then {
    onlyUsesInts(unknownRightResult) as int else{}
} else if unknownRightResult @istype ErrorList then {
    handleError(unknownRightResult) as ErrorList else{}
}

docs.title: Type Casting with as
docs.text:
The as keyword attempts to cast a union to a specific type. If the cast fails, the else block is executed:

var value :: int | string
value is "hello"

# This will execute the else block since value is currently a string
const number is value as int else {
    return error.ExpectedInteger
}

# This will succeed since value is now an int
value is 42
const doubled is value as int else {
    return error.ExpectedInteger
} # doubled is 84

as can be used for control flow as well, using then blocks:

# using as like an 'istype' style conditional
asThenUnion as int then {
    var result is 20 + 30
    result?
} else {
    var result is 30 + 40
    result?
} # 50

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text:
Safe extraction with default:

const result is someUnion as int else {
    return 0 # Default value if not an int
}

Error handling:

const number is value as int else {
    @panic("This should never happen in production!")
}

Conditional processing:

const processed is value as string else {
    # Handle non-string case
    return "default"
}

The as keyword is essential for safely working with unions when you need to extract a specific type.

docs.title: Zig
docs.text:
zig blocks are embedded Zig modules.

Zig can be brought into a Doxa program two ways, both subject to the same rules below:

  • Inline block — zig <Name> { ... } defines module <Name> directly in the .doxa source.
  • File import — module <Alias> from "<path>.zig" imports an external .zig file as module <Alias>.

Both forms are validated by the same extractor and lower to the same code generation and ABI path, so <Name>.func(...) calls behave identically regardless of form.

docs.title: File imports
docs.text:
module Math from "mathutil.zig"

const n is Math.double(21)
  • The import alias (Math) names the module; calls use Alias.func(...).
  • The path resolves relative to the importing .doxa file, like any other module ... from import.
  • The imported file must obey the restricted subset below; violations are reported as a compile error (E7010).
  • Edits to the imported .zig are picked up automatically on the next build — the generated module is content-hashed (together with the toolchain, target, and optimization level) and rebuilt whenever any of those changes, so no manual cache clearing is needed.

docs.title: Importing Zig into a block
docs.text:
An inline block may @import a .zig file beside the .doxa file that declares it, and call into it:

enum Fail { Negative }

zig Calc {
    const engine = @import("calc/engine.zig");

    pub fn twice(x: i64) DoxaError_Fail!i64 {
        return engine.twice(x);
    }
}
  • The path resolves relative to the declaring .doxa file; a file that is not there is reported at the block (E7001).
  • The imported file is plain Zig: any top-level declarations, its own state, and imports of further files beside it. It is not a Doxa module and names no Doxa type; the block is its Doxa surface. So an engine can keep its own Zig error sets, and the block's DoxaError_<path> set checks, by name, that every error it passes on is a variant of the Doxa enum.
  • Each imported file is compiled as a Zig module of the name the block spells, read in place. Its content, and that of every file it imports in turn, keys the block's object, so an edit to any of them rebuilds it.
  • A Zig compile error in an imported file is reported at that file's line (E7015).

This is the form to use when a block needs more than functions, or when its Zig deserves a file of its own (std.http is one). A .zig file imported directly with module ... from stays limited to the rules below.

docs.title: Current source-level rules
docs.text:
1. Top-level is restricted to:
  2. const X = @import("...");

  3. fn ... { ... }

  4. Function signatures are restricted to Doxa-compatible types:

  5. Doxa int <-> Zig i64
  6. Doxa float <-> Zig f64
  7. Doxa byte <-> Zig u8
  8. Doxa tetra <-> Zig bool (lossy at boundary)
  9. Doxa nothing <-> Zig void
  10. Doxa string <-> Zig []const u8
  11. Doxa int[] <-> Zig []const i64
  12. Doxa float[] <-> Zig []const f64
  13. Doxa byte[] <-> Zig []const DoxaByte (DoxaByte is an injected alias for u8)
  14. Doxa string[] <-> Zig []const []const u8
  15. Doxa T[][] <-> additional []const levels (nesting is unlimited)
  16. Doxa enum <-> Zig DoxaEnum_<name> (an injected alias for i64; the value is the variant's discriminant)
  17. Doxa enum[] <-> Zig []const DoxaEnum_<name>
  18. Doxa struct <- Zig DoxaStruct_<name>, as a result only (see Struct results)
  19. Doxa T | <enum> <- Zig DoxaError_<name>!T, as a result only (see Error model)

Arrays of scalars, strings, and enums cross in both directions at any depth; the []const element slices a Zig function receives are borrowed for the call. A bare []const u8 is always a string, so byte arrays use the DoxaByte marker. A Doxa enum crosses as its i64 variant discriminant, spelled DoxaEnum_<path> where <path> names the enum through the bindings of the file declaring the zig block — DoxaEnum_Color for its own enum Color. A qualified path is spelled as a Zig quoted identifier: after import error from @std(), std's Method enum is @"DoxaEnum_error.Method". The wrapper declares every spelling it finds as i64, so the Zig author compares against integers. A .zig file has no Doxa bindings, so naming a DoxaEnum_ there is a located error. See Array parameters and returns for the ownership rules.

  1. The compiler validates these rules before invoking Zig.

docs.title: Inline Zig ABI
docs.text: Each module compiles to an object file exporting one symbol per signature, named by the function's mangled link name, and the LLVM backend declares and calls those symbols directly. A zig block is a module of its own, owned by the file that declares it, so two files may each declare zig Math { pub fn double … }: their functions are distinct symbols. The wrapper object is linked into the program next to the runtime — nothing is loaded or looked up at run time (no dlopen, no GetProcAddress), and doxa run and doxa compile build the same objects and issue the same calls.

docs.title: Generated wrapper
docs.text:
For a Doxa-visible fn f, the generator emits:

pub fn __doxa_native__f(a0: T0, …) callconv(.c) R { … }
// or, when f returns a string or an array (see "The caller's arena"):
pub fn __doxa_native__f(__doxa_scope: *Scope, a0: T0, …) callconv(.c) R { … }
comptime { @export(&__doxa_native__f, .{ .name = "<link name of f>" }); }

A link name has the form __doxa_m1_<tag>__f<len>$<name>: <tag> is a hash of the declaring module's stable key, and every component is length-prefixed, so no two declarations in a program share one. Diagnostics, peek, and reflection show the declared name, never the link name.

The wrapper is the root of its object, and it declares std_options, so a zig block may not declare its own. It sets unexpected_error_tracing = false: an OS status Zig's standard library does not recognise is still returned as error.Unexpected, but no Zig stack trace is printed to the program's stderr. The runtime's root does the same.

The body is a thin adapter from the ABI types below to the user's Zig signature: it re-slices string parameters and, for string returns, performs the arena clone described under ownership. There is no argument vector, no tag decoding, and no status code.

docs.title: The caller's arena
docs.text: A function whose result is a heap value — a string or an array, including the payload of a fallible return — builds it in the caller's arena, which the caller passes as a hidden first argument, __doxa_scope: *Scope, before the declared parameters. Every other function takes no hidden argument. The rule is one predicate (takesArena in src/inline_zig/compiler.zig) that the wrapper generator and the LLVM backend both read. The arena is the call site's innermost open scope, the same arena a Doxa function's result would live in; the wrapper never names a scope the caller did not hand it.

docs.title: Passing rules (fixed 64-bit lengths)
docs.text:
• Scalars pass as their Zig types: int → i64, float → f64, byte → u8, tetra → bool, nothing → void.
  • A string parameter passes as (ptr, u64 len) — a pointer followed by a fixed 64-bit byte length — and the wrapper re-slices it to []const u8.
  • A string return writes through out_ptr: *?[*]u8, out_len: *u64 — two out-params, not a (ptr, len) return pair. The empty string crosses as (null, 0) and allocates nothing.
  • The runtime's exported string helpers (doxa_str_*, doxa_*_to_string, …) use the same fixed 64-bit len: u64 / *u64 for lengths and byte counts.

Lengths are 64-bit on every target so the emitted LLVM IR — which declares %DoxaString = { ptr, i64 } and i64 length parameters — needs no target-specific rewriting. Pointers keep the target's pointer width; a pointer that meets a 64-bit length slot is widened or narrowed with @intCast / @intFromPtr.

docs.title: String rule
docs.text:
• Strings cross as pointer + byte length, never as C-strings.
  • Embedded \0 is valid and must be preserved.

docs.title: Ownership and lifetime
docs.text:
• String parameters are borrowed for the duration of the call.
  • A returned string lands in the caller's arena: the wrapper clones the bytes into __doxa_scope with doxa_str_clone, so the value follows the ordinary arena rules in memory.md — bulk-freed with its scope, and no free hook.
  • Non-string returns cross by value.
  • A module may keep process-lifetime Zig-owned state (the std.json node table, the std.http client and connection tables) provided it never retains a Doxa arena pointer across calls: values crossing in are borrowed for the call, copied with an owned allocation if they must outlive it, and every owned buffer is released explicitly, since arena scopes do not cover Zig-owned memory.

docs.title: Array parameters and returns
docs.text:
• An array crosses as an opaque *ArrayHeader pointer. The compile-time element type in the signature fixes the runtime elem_size / elem_tag; the two must agree.
  • An array parameter is borrowed for the call. The wrapper presents it to Zig as a []const T — scalar and byte[] arrays alias the array's backing buffer, string[] is copied into a temporary per-call arena, and nested arrays recurse through that arena. The callee must not retain or store it.
  • A returned []const T is copied into a fresh ArrayHeader in the caller's arena (doxa_array_new(__doxa_scope, …)), so it follows the same arena rules as a returned string. Nested levels are deep-cloned as they are stored.

docs.title: Struct results
docs.text:
A Zig function may return a Doxa struct, spelled DoxaStruct_<path>, where <path> names the struct through the bindings of the file declaring the zig block, as for DoxaEnum_ (@"DoxaStruct_ns.Run" for a qualified path). The Zig code declares nothing: the wrapper generates the mirror from the Doxa declaration, with the same field names and the types of the table above, so the body builds it like any Zig struct and the two cannot drift.

struct Run {
    public status :: int,
    output :: string,
}

zig Proc {
    pub fn run() DoxaStruct_Run {
        return .{ .status = 0, .output = "done" };
    }
}
  • Plain data only. Every field is a scalar, string, enum, an array of those, or another struct that follows these rules. A union, group, function value, or array of structs is refused (E8002), naming the field.
  • Results only. A struct parameter is refused (E8002); pass its fields.
  • Private fields. The wrapper sets a private field only in a struct the file declaring the block declares, as that file's own struct literal could. A struct from another file must have only public fields.
  • Ownership. The struct, and every string and array it holds, is built in the caller's arena. It is a fresh value that follows the ordinary arena rules (docs/memory.md).
  • Layout stays with Doxa. The bridge never writes a Doxa struct. It hands each field back through an out-parameter of its own (a nested struct's fields in turn), and the caller builds the struct the way a struct literal is built.
  • A .zig file has no Doxa bindings, so it cannot name a DoxaStruct_.

docs.title: Error model
docs.text:
A Zig function can fail into Doxa by returning DoxaError_<path>!T, where <path> names a Doxa enum as for DoxaEnum_. The wrapper declares a Zig error set of that name holding the enum's variants, so the body returns error.<Variant>. Doxa sees T | <enum>, the error as the enum variant of the same name, and narrows it with as or match like any union. T may be void (nothing), i64, string, an array, or a DoxaStruct_. On failure nothing of T is built.

No other error crosses: a Zig function that cannot fail returns its value, and one that panics ends the program. Unions, groups, and functions do not cross the boundary (E8002). A Zig function is not a value Doxa can hold or pass; Doxa only calls the exported functions.

docs.title: Hello World
docs.text: Let's start with three ways we can print the string "Hello World" to the screen.

docs.title: Peek Operator
docs.text:
Doxa uses a question mark symbol as a shorthand form of print debugging. Any value can be appended with ? and the program will return the file, line number, value name (if it exists), type, and value. Here we will simply peek at the string literal.

"Hello World"?

[my_file.doxa:1:14] :: string is "Hello World"
Notice that there is no value name associated with this string. We can see the difference by assigning to to a variable first. 
var hello is "Hello World"
hello?

[my_file.doxa:2:6] hello :: string is "Hello World"
Peeking is a safe operation with no side effects and can be done without any risk of runtime errors.

docs.title: Intrinsic Print
docs.text:
There is also an intrinsic print method provided at compiler level. All intrinsic methods are prefixed with the @ symbol. The @print method does what it says, takes a string and prints it to the screen.

@print("Hello World")

Hello World
Note that line breaks must be handled manually with @print.

@print("Hello World")
@print("Hello World")

Hello WorldHello World
Intrinsic methods like @print are unsafe, and so improper use can cause unexpected errors including crashes. This should be kept in mind whenever using compiler level intrinsic methods.

docs.title: Standard Library
docs.text:
The standard library provides safe print functions in the io module. Here we will use io.println. This function handles new lines in a cross platform friendly way so we don't have to worry about manually inserting line breaks.

module std from @std()
std.io.println("Hello World")
std.io.println("Hello World")

Hello World
Hello World
If we peek at the values returned we can see that the intrinsic @print() method simply returns nothing, while std.io.println returns a union of nothing | StdError. This is what lets us unwrap a failed function call safely. We will learn more about this when we look at unions. 
module std from @std()
var intrinsic_result is @print("Hello World\n")
intrinsic_result?
var std_result is std.io.println("Hello World")
std_result?

Hello World
[my_file.doxa:3:17] intrinsic_result :: nothing is nothing
Hello World
[my_file.doxa:5:11] std_result :: >nothing | StdError is nothing

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
In Doxa variables are assigned and reassigned using the keyword is. This was chosen over an = because of the bugs inherent to confusing assignment = with equality ==. By disallowing single = we avoid this class of error entirely.

Doxa has two kinds of variable declaration, var which is mutable, and const which is constant. All variable declarations will be prefaced with one of these two keywords.

var x is 5
const y is 10
x is x + y
x?

[./my_file.doxa:4:2] x :: int is 15
If we tried to reassign the variable y, which is marked constant, we would get the following error: 
DoxVM: [CompileTime][Error][E1015] ./my_file.doxa:3:1: Cannot assign to immutable variable 'y'
   2 | const y is 10
   3 | y is x + y
     | ^ Error: Cannot assign to immutable variable 'y'
   4 | y?

docs.title: Typing
docs.text:
When declaring a variable, a type inference will be made. If you would like a variable to be uninitiallized, it must be provided a type using ::. All variables have static types known at compile time meaning you cannot reassign a variable to a value of a different type.

var x :: int is 5
var y is 5 # this is inferred as an int
var z :: int # this is initialized with a default value of 0

Uninitialized variables are given a default value depending on their type. Read the doc page for more details.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Doxa was designed to have a minimal number of native types which can be composed into higher more complex data structures. Here are the scalar types and their default values.

When we talk about size below, we mean what a value of that type occupies as its own payload in the native compiler path (roughly: what you would expect in a local or on the operand stack after lowering): fixed-width numbers, a discriminant for enums, or a reference for heap-backed data. It is not the byte length of string contents, array storage, or struct fields—those live on the heap (or in separate storage) and grow with your data.

Scalars

Type Value representation Default value int 64-bit signed integer 0 float 64-bit IEEE binary float 0.0 byte 8-bit unsigned integer 0 (0x00) string Reference to UTF-8 text elsewhere "" tetra 2-bit unsigned integer false enum Discriminant as an integer index nothing No payload nothing

The doxa run VM represents values with more bookkeeping than the table above (for example enum variants carry type names for introspection), but the logical sizes and defaults match the native path. If you embed Doxa and exchange values through the C-facing runtime, values are passed as a tagged DoxaValue (tag + reserved flags + 64-bit payload); see doxa_rt.zig in the repo for the exact ABI.

docs.title: Array
docs.text: Arrays are strictly typed, you must provide a single type for an array. Arrays of composite types like arrays, structs, etc. are supported. If arrays are sized in their type declaration such as: var x :: int[64] the size is fixed.

docs.title: Struct
docs.text:
Structs are named records with fields, functions, and methods. Doxa has no classes and no inheritance—you model “is-a” relationships by composition (a struct field whose type is another struct). Fields and callables are private unless marked public.

Struct literals must use the $ prefix: $MyStruct { ... }. An identifier immediately followed by { is not a struct literal; it is parsed as an implicit match pattern, so forgetting $ is a common early mistake. Struct values are allocated from the current scope’s arena. See Structs for construction, methods, and performance notes.

docs.title: Group
docs.text: A group is a nominal umbrella over existing enum, struct, and other group types: it re-exports their variants and fields under qualified names (for example Error.IOError.NotFound) without introducing new runtime values. Use it when a function or API should accept “one of these known alternatives” as a single type. Flattening, uniqueness, and cycle rules matter once groups grow; see Groups.

docs.title: Union
docs.text:
Typed unions are written with | between types, for example int | float or string | nothing for an optional string. A union variable holds one member type at a time; if you do not initialize it, it defaults to the first type in the union with that type’s default value.

To react to which member is active, use match (exhaustive branches narrow the type), value as T else { ... } for a single-arm cast with a fallback, or @istype in if / else if chains when you need imperative style. See Typed unions for patterns, including error-style returns.

docs.title: Numeric conversions
docs.text:
Numeric types (int, float, byte) convert implicitly in some contexts and require explicit casts in others. The goal is to prevent silent data loss while avoiding noise for obviously-safe conversions.

Direction Operator position Value position Requires byte → int implicit implicit nothing — always lossless int → byte — comptime literals only @byte() for runtime values int → float implicit comptime literals only @float() for runtime or named const values byte → float implicit comptime literals only @float() for runtime or named const values

Operator positions (binary +, -, *, /, etc.) promote automatically via the numeric lattice: float > int > byte.

Value positions (assignment, function arguments, return values, struct fields) allow widening only when the right-hand side is a literal written directly in source. Named constants and runtime variables must use the explicit intrinsic.

var f :: float is 10          # allowed — literal 10 widens to 10.0
takesFloat(10)                # allowed — literal 10 widens to 10.0
float[] is [1, 2, 3]         # allowed — each element is a literal

const LIT is 10
takesFloat(LIT)               # error — use @float(LIT)

var i :: int is 10
takesFloat(i)                 # error — use @float(i)

var b :: byte is 200
var i2 :: int is b            # allowed — byte → int is always lossless

Conversion intrinsics: @float(), @int(), @byte(), @string(). See Intrinsic Methods.
